title: Block B close: the generation
hook: slaves and merchants, poets and nurses, women and men, all of them learners

segments.voice: Yesterday, Salim, the freed man the Prophet named among four to learn the Qur'an from. Your line was: learn from these four. Who did you thank? Day eight hundred sixty-two.

Lay them out on a table like photographs. A merchant who spent his wealth buying people out of slavery. A man of Abyssinian descent who had been one of those people, calling the prayer. A Persian who traveled from teacher to teacher looking for the truth. A poet. A nurse in a tent. A woman who taught writing. A woman who asked for a day. A shepherd who became a reciter. A man from Yemen who stayed home with his mother. If someone handed you that pile and said, this is one generation, you might ask what holds it together. Today we close the block on the companions.
screen: `A MERCHANT, A CALLER, A SEEKER.` → `A POET, A NURSE, A TEACHER.` → `WHAT HOLDS THEM TOGETHER?`

segments.voice: We started this block with a question: who is a companion? A sahabi, in the common Sunni definition, is someone who met the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, as a believer, and died a believer. That's a wide door, and the people who came through it were not chosen for their background. Walk back through them. The first circle: Abu Bakr and his purchases, Umar walking at night, Uthman and the well of Rumah, Ali and his words. The mothers of the believers: Khadijah, Aisha the scholar, Hafsah keeping the pages, Umm Salamah and the others. The family: Fatimah and her hands, Hasan the peacemaker, Husayn. Then Bilal, Salman, Abu Dharr, Ammar, Mus'ab, Zayd, Usamah, Umm Ayman. The reciters: Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy, Zayd ibn Thabit, Mu'adh. And this last stretch: Abu Hurayrah and Anas, Nusaybah at Uhud, Asma and her two belts, Rufaydah's tent, al-Shifa teaching writing, Umm Sulaym, Hassan the poet, Ka'b who told the truth, Suhayb, Khabbab the blacksmith, Abu Ayyub the host, Sa'd, Abu Musa, Hudhayfah and Salim. And Uways, who by that definition was not a companion at all, since he never met the Prophet, yet whose story sits among theirs. So what holds them together? Look back at story after story and you'll find someone learning. Asking a question. Memorizing a verse. Asking for a day. Asking about harm. Standing behind whoever knew the most Qur'an. Read this way, the companions look like a generation of students. One more honest thing. Muslims don't all remember every one of these names the same way. Sunni and Shia Muslims hold different views about some companions, especially around what happened after the Prophet's death. The next block begins exactly there, and it will set out each telling in its own words.
screen: `WHO IS A COMPANION?` · `THE NAMES, WALKED BACK.` · `NEARLY EVERY STORY, A LEARNER.` · `REMEMBERED IN MORE THAN ONE WAY.` · then, large: `ORDINARY PEOPLE, EXTRAORDINARY FAITH.`

segments.voice: The practice: write the names you remember. Take a piece of paper, or your notes app. Without looking anything up, write down every companion from this block you can recall. Next to each name, write one thing: a word, a scene, an object. A belt. A tent. A well. A pipe. A mother. Don't worry about the ones you've lost. When the list feels done, read it back slowly. If you pray, you can use the words Muslims say after a companion's name: may God be pleased with them. The bell holds the time.

Sahabi, a companion of the Prophet: someone who met him as a believer and died a believer. This block's close: a generation of very different people, held together by learning and faith. Today's word.
Your line: ordinary people, extraordinary faith. Today, tell one person the story of one companion from your list. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the lives of the companions in sermons, classes and family storytelling, and say 'may God be pleased with him' or 'with her' after a companion's name.
